title: How the Gender Pay Gap Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the gender pay gap in the United States and worldwide, timed around Equal Pay Day (April 12, 2016). They cover the history of wage disparity, how the earnings ratio is calculated (median full-time earnings) and why it is criticized as apples-to-oranges, occupational clustering and segregation, racial differences in the pay gap, Bureau of Labor Statistics data, a Glassdoor study of equally qualified employees, pay secrecy and the #TalkPay campaign, government responses (Obama's 2014 executive order, California pay transparency law, Equal Pay Act of 1963, Title VII), the Lilly Ledbetter v. Goodyear case and the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, economic explanations such as the care penalty and temporal flexibility drawn from a Freakonomics episode, and state-by-state differences. Listener mail closes the episode.
topics: Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data

segments.title: Sponsor read and opening
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Squarespace, then the hosts introduce the episode and mention Equal Pay Day.

segments.title: Equal Pay Day and history of the pay gap
segments.summary: The hosts explain Equal Pay Day, the long history of women earning less than men in the US, and the stagnation of the gap since the 1963 Equal Pay Act. They note the gap's costs over a career and that its causes are debated.

segments.title: Racial differences and the earnings ratio
segments.summary: Pay gaps differ by race and ethnicity, with Asian women earning more relative to white men than other groups. The hosts explain how the earnings ratio is computed from median full-time salaries and why critics call it apples-to-oranges.

segments.title: Occupational clustering and segregation
segments.summary: Most working women are concentrated in about twenty fields, and jobs dominated by women tend to pay less. Even within the same occupation, men tend to earn more. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show that most occupations still pay men more, though some pay women more.
topics: Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data

segments.title: Glassdoor study and pay transparency
segments.summary: A Glassdoor study of employee salary reports found equally qualified women earn about five percent less than men at the same company, with the largest gap among computer scientists. Pay secrecy and company rules against discussing salaries limit awareness. The #TalkPay hashtag and the TalkPay site encouraged salary sharing.

segments.title: Laws: executive order, California, Equal Pay Act, Title VII, and Ledbetter case
segments.summary: Obama's 2014 executive order barred federal contractors from punishing employees for discussing pay. California passed a law on pay transparency and substantially-equal pay. The hosts review Lilly Ledbetter's Goodyear case, the 180-day filing limit, the Supreme Court's 5-4 decision, Ginsburg's dissent, and the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act.

segments.title: Causes: care penalty, temporal flexibility, and policy fixes
segments.summary: Drawing on a Freakonomics episode, economists Claudia Goldin and Anne-Marie Slaughter attribute much of the remaining gap to the care penalty and temporal flexibility, not proven discrimination. Parental leave, school hours, and state-by-state differences are discussed, with Washington, D.C. having the smallest gap and Louisiana the largest.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener Jason Tardy writes about nostalgia from a trail run. The hosts sign off with contact information and a pointer to howstuffworks.com.
